**A balanced, practical approach** Below is a step‑by‑step proposal you can present to the head‑teacher (and, if needed, to the cantonal education office). It tries to honour the family’s religious request while keeping the swimming programme inclusive, educationally sound, and in line with Swiss school law. --- ### 1. Clarify the legal and curricular framework | Point | What it means for you | |-------|-----------------------| | **Swiss school law (Kanton Aargau)** | Physical education, including swimming, is compulsory. Schools may grant *reasonable* accommodations for sincere religious convictions, provided the core learning objectives are still met. | | **Curriculum goal for swimming (Primary‑level)** | • Basic water‑safety skills (floating, kicking, breath control).
• Development of motor coordination and confidence in water.
• Social interaction in a mixed‑gender setting (optional, not the sole aim). | | **Principle of proportionality** | Any exemption or alternative must be the *least restrictive* means of achieving the curricular goals. | > **Take‑away:** You can offer a modified participation model (different attire, separate time, or parallel activity) as long as the pupil still acquires the essential water‑safety competencies. --- ### 2. Gather the family’s specific concerns A brief, respectful conversation (you or a school‑social‑worker) can clarify: * Is the objection to *mixed‑gender* water exposure, to *showing skin* in a swimsuit, or both? * Would a modest‑coverage garment (e.g., a burkini, full‑length swim shirt + leggings) alleviate the issue? * Are they open to the child attending the same pool but at a different time slot, or to a supervised, gender‑separate session? Document the answers (with parental consent) so you can show the head‑teacher that the request is concrete and not a blanket refusal. --- ### 3. Propose a tiered solution (choose the first that works) | Option | How it meets the goals | Practical notes for Aargau schools | |--------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------| | **A. Modest swimwear** (burkini, long‑sleeve rash guard + leggings) | Allows the girl to stay in the same mixed class, satisfying the social‑integration aim while respecting modesty. | Many Swiss pools already accept burkinis; check the pool’s dress‑code policy. Provide a spare set if the family does not own one. | | **B. Separate‑gender time slot** (e.g., girls‑only session) | Removes mixed‑gender contact while keeping the same water‑safety curriculum. | If the pool schedule permits, allocate a 15‑20 minute block either before or after the regular class. Coordinate with the pool manager; this is a common accommodation in many cantons. | | **C. Parallel water‑safety activity** (theory + dry‑land drills) | Guarantees the pupil learns the *core* safety knowledge (hazards, rescue basics, breathing techniques) even if she does not enter the water. | Use the school’s gym or classroom for:
• Video demonstrations of safe entry/exit.
• Practice of flutter kicks and arm motions on dry land.
• Simple quizzes or worksheets on water‑danger signs.
She can join the mixed class for the final 5‑minute “cool‑down” or a group game on the pool edge if she feels comfortable. | | **D. Exemption with compensatory activity** (only if A‑C are impossible) | The pupil is excused from the swimming block but must complete an alternative PE unit of equal duration (e.g., gymnastics, dance, or a coordinated games module) that meets the same PE learning outcomes. | Must be approved by the head‑teacher and recorded in the pupil’s individual learning plan. This is the *last resort* because it reduces water‑specific skill acquisition. | **Recommendation:** Start with **Option A** (modest swimwear). If the family objects to any exposed skin even with a burkini, move to **Option B** (separate‑gender slot). Only consider **C** or **D** if the pool cannot accommodate a separate slot and the family refuses modest attire. --- ### 4. Outline the implementation plan (to show the head‑teacher) 1. **Contact the pool manager** (within 3 days) to confirm: * Acceptance of burkinis or other modest swimwear. * Availability of a girls‑only slot (if needed) and any extra cost. 2. **Prepare a short information sheet** for the class (age‑appropriate) explaining why a classmate may wear different swimwear or swim at a different time — focus on respect and diversity, not on the religion itself. 3. **Arrange a trial day** (one lesson) where the girl wears the agreed attire or attends the separate slot. Observe: * Her comfort level. * Any reactions from peers (address with a brief classroom discussion if needed). * Whether she can demonstrate the required safety skills (e.g., floating, basic kick). 4. **Document outcomes** (photos with permission, teacher notes) and share a brief report with the head‑teacher after 2‑3 weeks. 5. **Review and adjust**: If the solution works, make it the standing arrangement for the remainder of the swimming unit. If not, move to the next tier in the proposal. --- ### 5. Communication tips (to keep the climate positive) * **Frame the request as an accommodation, not a privilege.** Emphasise that the goal is to ensure every child can meet the curriculum objectives. * **Use inclusive language:** “We are looking for a way that lets *all* pupils learn water safety while respecting personal beliefs.” * **Invite the parents to observe a lesson** (if they wish) so they can see the safety focus and the modest attire in action. * **Involve the school’s integration officer or cantonal advisory service** (if available) for additional support and to ensure compliance with Aargau’s integration guidelines. --- ### 6. Quick checklist for your proposal document - [ ] Summary of the family’s concern (modesty / mixed gender). - [ ] Reference to Aargau school law & swimming curriculum objectives. - [ ] Description of the proposed accommodation (starting with modest swimwear). - [ ] Steps for implementation (pool contact, trial, documentation). - [ ] Fallback options (separate slot, parallel activity, compensatory PE). - [ ] Timeline (e.g., decision within one week, trial within two weeks). - [ ] Expected outcome: pupil achieves water‑safety competencies; class maintains inclusive environment. --- ### Final thought The aim is **not** to let the girl miss out on essential water‑safety learning, nor to force her into a situation that conflicts with her family’s sincere beliefs. By offering a modest‑attire option first — and having clear, pre‑agreed alternatives — you demonstrate respect for diversity while upholding the school’s educational mandate. Presenting the proposal in this structured, evidence‑based way will make it easier for the head‑teacher to approve and for the pool staff to implement. Good luck, and feel free to ask if you need a sample email to the pool manager or a brief classroom handout on respecting differences!
